content: 1. The 2016 update of the WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) aimed to revise the evidence-based policy recommendations from 2011. The scope of the 2016 guidelines was narrower than the 2011 version, focusing on specific priority areas in the treatment and care of patients with drug-resistant TB. 2. The 2016 guidelines emphasized the optimal combination of medicines and approaches for designing treatment regimens for patients with isoniazid-resistant TB, rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), and Mycobacterium bovis disease. 3. The guidelines also evaluated the effectiveness and safety of standardized shorter regimens lasting up to 12 months for MDR-TB treatment compared to longer regimens. Additionally, they assessed the impact of delayed treatment initiation and surgical interventions on treatment outcomes for drug-resistant TB. 4. The target audience for these guidelines includes healthcare professionals involved in TB prevention and care, program managers implementing drug-resistant TB management, and organizations providing technical and financial support. While primarily intended for resource-limited settings, the recommendations are applicable in other contexts as well. 5. The guidelines used the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework to address key questions. These questions were grouped into four sets, each corresponding to specific areas of the guideline's scope. The outcomes were scored by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) on a scale of 1 to 9, with scores of 7–9 considered critical for making recommendations. 6. The certainty of evidence was categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. High certainty indicates that further research is unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate, while very low certainty reflects significant uncertainty in the effect estimate. 7. Recommendations were classified as either strong or conditional. Strong recommendations indicate that the desirable effects of adherence outweigh the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations suggest that the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects. The strength of a recommendation depends on the quality of evidence, balance of effects, values and preferences, and resource considerations. 8. For patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB who had not been previously treated with second-line drugs and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents was excluded, shorter MDR-TB regimens lasting 9–12 months were recommended. These regimens are largely standardized and based on documented evidence from various settings. 9. Longer MDR-TB regimens, lasting 18 months or more, may be standardized or individualized. These regimens typically include a minimum number of second-line TB medicines considered effective based on patient history or drug-resistance patterns. They were previously referred to as conventional regimens and were the mainstay of MDR-TB treatment before the 2016 update. 10. The guidelines also addressed the use of second-line TB medicines, including bedaquiline and delamanid, and provided new policy guidance on the use of line probe assays for detecting resistance to second-line anti-TB drugs. 11. The GDG assessed evidence using systematic literature reviews and individual patient-level data. Relative effects (e.g., relative risks or odds ratios) and absolute effects (e.g., risk differences) were calculated to express the magnitude of differences between intervention and comparator groups. Adjustments were made to reduce bias and confounding where possible. 12. The GDG considered the spectrum of values and preferences of different users when formulating recommendations. Variability in these values and preferences was a key factor that lowered the strength of all recommendations in the guidelines. 13. Resource use was assessed from the perspectives of patients and health services, focusing on feasibility and opportunity costs rather than formal cost-effectiveness studies. 14. The guidelines underwent external review, with substantive comments provided by six reviewers. The final recommendations were made available as freely downloadable PDF files and in print versions to ensure wide dissemination. 15. The WHO plans to reflect the changes in these guidelines in a forthcoming revision of the implementation handbook for programmatic management of drug-resistant TB. The organization will work with regional and country offices, as well as technical and funding agencies, to ensure effective communication of the updated guidance. 16. The guidelines highlight the importance of further research to address gaps in evidence and improve the management of drug-resistant TB. The GDG identified research priorities within the dimensions covered by each PICO question. This explanation provides a detailed and professional summary of the content, ensuring clarity and precision for medical professionals and stakeholders.
